extracted.intended_audience: public administration scholars, social scientists, and policymakers studying human–algorithm interaction and algorithmic decision-making in the public sector
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating algorithmic advice in public decisions
extracted.subtask_description: Empirically assess how human decision-makers process algorithmic versus human-expert advice in public-sector decision contexts, testing for automation bias and selective adherence using randomized experimental designs and regression analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: "Decision-makers would automatically default to the algorithm, potentially then also to poor algorithmic advice, ignoring contradictory cues from other sources: automation bias."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual criterion for evaluating whether participants follow algorithmic outputs more than human advice. The article operationalizes this by comparing adherence rates to ILE scores generated by algorithm versus human experts across three studies; notes that absence of higher adherence to algorithm indicates lack of automation bias. Also compares to prior domains (aviation, healthcare) where automation bias is documented and discusses exposure/trust as mediating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective adherence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Decision-makers’ tendency to defer to the algorithm selectively—when algorithmic predictions match pre-existing stereotypes: selective adherence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether advice (human or algorithmic) is followed disproportionately when it aligns with stereotypes (e.g., teacher ethnicity). The paper tests this via a teacher ethnicity manipulation and examines main effects and interactions with advice type; finds selective adherence occurs across both advice sources and may not be exacerbated by algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare algorithmic advice with equivalent human advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological standard: previous studies often failed to compare algorithmic advice with equivalent human advice; this study remedies that omission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing automation bias or selective adherence, experimental designs should present algorithmic advice and human-expert advice that are substantively equivalent so differences in adherence can be attributed to source (algorithm vs human) rather than to differences in content or quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary outcome: following the ILE score (measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Note: Binary outcome: following the ILE score (1 = non-renewal of employment of teacher with lowest ILE score).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, pre-specified outcome measures (here, a binary indicator of whether participant selects the teacher with lowest ILE score). Report descriptive percentages and model-based estimates (odds ratios, confidence intervals, z, p).

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomization and factorial design (advice × ethnicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use randomization groups and a factorial design to manipulate advice source (algorithmic vs human-expert) and teacher ethnicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomize participants into experimental conditions; use factorial layout to test main effects and interactions (e.g., Algorithm × Moroccan-Dutch teacher). Report regression results for main effects and interaction terms with appropriate inference (ORs, CIs, z, p).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions and attention checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusions: Participants who failed the attention check or completed the questionnaire in less than 3 min. ** Participants not of Dutch descent (excluded from the analysis of selective adherence hypotheses—H2 and H3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement attention checks and minimum completion time filters; pre-specify and report exclusion rules. For subgroup-specific hypotheses, restrict the sample appropriately (e.g., toDutch-descent respondents when testing ethnicity-based selective adherence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include covariates and robustness checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Including covariates and restricting the sample to those who successfully completed the manipulation checks does not change the results (supplementary tables A5.1.1 and A5.2.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct robustness checks by adding control variables and by re-running analyses on cleaned subsamples to verify stability of results; report supplementary tables with these checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess interactions with demographics and representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The interactions between the advice manipulation and participants’ gender, age and higher education are all statistically insignificant. This suggests that a sample more representative of the civil service’s demographic and socioeconomic characteristics would have yielded similar results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether treatment effects vary by key demographics (gender, age, education). Evaluate and report representativeness of sample relative to the target population (e.g., civil service) and discuss implications for external validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure participants’ familiarity / prior exposure to algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: The negative effect of the algorithmic advice is linked to respondents’ reported familiarity with the use of algorithms by public organizations. When filtering our sample in study 3 to participants who were not familiar with the use of algorithms by public organizations before the survey..., the likelihood of following the algorithmic advice increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect measures of participants' prior awareness/familiarity with algorithm use (including exposure to scandals) and use these as moderators or control variables to explain heterogeneity in adherence/trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for social desirability and sample source effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A methodological explanation ... is that civil servant participants’ responses could reflect social desirability bias ... This threat is plausibly more likely for the sample of professional civil servants ... invited by a panel linked to the Dutch government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider and discuss potential social desirability bias especially in professional or government-linked samples; design surveys to mitigate (anonymity assurances, indirect questioning) and interpret null findings cautiously when such bias may be present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report full statistical details and model fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Regression tables report OR [95% CI], z, p value, Observations, Log-likelihood, BIC, AIC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide complete regression output including effect estimates with confidence intervals, test statistics, p-values, sample size, and model fit indices (log-likelihood, BIC, AIC) to allow readers to evaluate evidence strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine domain differences and generalizability across fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare findings to automation bias literature in aviation and healthcare where automation bias is documented; explain domain-specific differences (routine use, exposure to reliable automation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When generalizing results, consider domain-specific histories of automation use and user exposure; do not assume findings in one administrative context will map directly onto high-automation sectors like aviation or healthcare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish bias at algorithm-output level versus human–AI interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: While algorithms’ outputs themselves could be bias-free, bias can also crop up at another level: in the human–AI interaction, in how decision-makers process, interpret, and act upon algorithmic outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both the fairness/performance of algorithmic outputs and the behavioral responses of human decision-makers; designs should separate these channels to understand how human processing may introduce or amplify bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep humans-in-the-loop and legal/regulatory safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping humans-in-the-loop (human intervention) is an important safeguard against algorithmic failures and is even legally mandated to that end in forward-looking regulatory frameworks such as the EU GDPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a policy guideline, maintain meaningful human oversight of automated decisions, ensure accountability and legal compliance (e.g., GDPR), and consider procedural protections to prevent harmful automated outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public exposure and transparency as corrective/learning mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: High-visibility, public exposure of such biases (as in the aftermath of the benefits scandal) can have learning effects through rendering civil servants more conscious and alert to such risks leading to their potential attenuation in decision making, at least in the short term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote transparency and public scrutiny of algorithmic deployments; monitor whether publicized failures change practitioner behavior and trust in algorithms; consider these dynamics when evaluating real-world adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate learning effects via repeated interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow-up work could further test the role of decision-makers’ learning and repeat exposure through a design that allows for repeat interactions with the algorithm so as to assess to what extent participants’ trust in the algorithm changes over time, potentially leading to patterns of enhanced deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing studies, include longitudinal or repeated-exposure components to capture how trust and deference evolve with experience. Consider implications for potential increases in automation deference over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sharing and transparency of materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The data underlying this article are available in Harvard Dataverse, at https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/TQYJNF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide access to underlying data and supplementary materials to enable replication and robustness checks; reference repository location and include supplementary tables (e.g., A5.x series) for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample reporting and comparison to population benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendix B provides sample characteristics and compares Dutch civil service data (2018) for representativeness (e.g., age, education percentages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report detailed sample demographics and, when possible, compare them to population benchmarks relevant for external validity (e.g., national civil service statistics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-registration / reporting of exclusions and hypothesis testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusions and hypothesis-specific sample restrictions are explicitly reported (attention checks, non-Dutch descent exclusion for H2/H3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-specify exclusions and hypothesis testing strategies; clearly report them in appendices so readers can assess potential analytic flexibility or selective reporting.
